newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese temple to open cemetery on the Internet.
newsitem.headline: Japanese temple to open cemetery on the Internet.

text.p: In Japan it will soon be possible to be virtually dead.
A Buddhist temple in the city of Hiroshima, western Japan, plans to open a "virtual graveyard" on the Internet.
Visitors will be able to choose different types of electronic tombstones and include photos of the deceased and family records on a Web page.
They will also be able to create their own memorials in advance and leave informal wills for their families.
Yukihiro Takada, a monk at the Kannonin temple, said the idea came from people who live too far away from the temple to visit but wanted to tend family memorials and pay respects to ancestors.
"After we announced we would offer a virtual cemetery, about 200 people asked to register, including Japanese people living overseas," Takada said.
He said they included people whose relatives" graves had been destroyed in the 1995 Kobe earthquake.
The virtual graveyard is expected to be launched on the temple"s homepage by the end of February and the temple will make no charge for putting "gravestones" on it.

Kannonin"s homepage (http://www.urban.or.jp/home/kanjizai/), at which visitors are greeted by the smiling face of the temple"s senior monk, already boasts about 20,000 retrievals a month, Takada said.
The Kannonin temple, belonging to the Shingon Buddhist sect, which has about 70,000 adherents, also runs an Internet cafe.
Takada said the temple had had requests for virtual graves for pets, such as dogs, cats and birds.
"Virtual" pets already have their own graveyard on the Kannonin homepage.

Electronic pet birds known as "Tamagocchi", which live on key-ring-sized, are the latest craze to sweep Japan. Tamagocchi owners must "feed", "play with" and "discipline" their pets, which "die" if not cared for properly.
The Tamagocchi graveyard page has had about 6,000 hits since the beginning of February.
